summary: On a tiny canvas with few colors, draw symmetric shapes at odd-numbered sizes so they have a true center, and give each extra color a specific job (highlight, edge softening, reflection).
takeaways: A 15x15 circle looks rounder than 16x16
Odd-numbered sides give clear median lines
Outline plus highlight alone can suggest bubble or cannonball
A third color softens edges or shows reflections

principles.principle: Draw small symmetric shapes at odd-numbered dimensions
principles.why: An odd size has a clear center (median) line, so at sprite scale a 15x15 circle reads as a truer circle than a 16x16 one.
principles.how: Draw circles at 15x15 inside a 16x16 sprite; in crafting games with broad units, build symmetric objects with odd-numbered sides.
principles.anti_pattern: Drawing tiny circles at even sizes with no center line.
principles.example: Kirby on Game Boy is a 16x16 sprite that Sakurai drew himself.
principles.quote: If you compare them, you'll see the 15x15 one is more of a true circle. That's because it has clear median lines.

principles.principle: Give each extra color a job: highlight, edge softening or reflection
principles.why: With just black and white, an outline and a highlight already distinguish a bubble from a cannonball; one more color lets you soften edges, which is essential for precise detail.
principles.how: Start from silhouette plus highlight, then add a third color for anti-aliased edges or a floor reflection on shiny material, chosen against the actual background color.
principles.anti_pattern: Shading a round object with a mesh pattern, which makes it look flat rather than round.
principles.quote: With just one more color, we're able to soften the edges. This technique is essential for more precise details.

summary: Treat game music as worth presenting on its own: when you curate a showcase, keep the performance in the spotlight, and size each edition so you can keep it going alongside your development work.
takeaways: PRESS START ran ten years of omnibus game music concerts
Game footage used sparingly so it never upstaged the performance
Each show: 14-16 pieces, about 60 songs counting medleys
Live music can stir emotions found nowhere else

principles.principle: Keep the performance central; use game footage only occasionally
principles.why: At PRESS START, playing video after video would have distracted from the point of the concert, the performance itself.
principles.how: In any music showcase, treat footage as an occasional accent and let the live music carry the event.
principles.anti_pattern: Running game video behind every piece.
principles.example: PRESS START game music concerts (2006-2016).

principles.principle: Fix a recurring project's run length and per-edition scope upfront
principles.why: Sakurai planned PRESS START for ten years from the start and saw it through; researching more songs than each program used would have been too much during game development.
principles.how: Before launching, decide the total run and the size of each edition (PRESS START: 14-16 program pieces, about 60 songs) so it fits beside your main work.
principles.anti_pattern: Open-ended side projects that grow until they compete with development.
principles.example: PRESS START, ten annual concerts, nearly all full houses.

principles.principle: Curate from a large candidate pool, then narrow down together
principles.why: As the committee member most familiar with games, Sakurai brought plenty of samples to meetings so the group could listen and narrow them down before arranging.
principles.how: Gather many more candidate tracks than you have slots, review them as a group, and only then commission arrangements.
principles.example: PRESS START song selection meetings.

summary: Cut the time between the player's "Ugh, I blew it!" and getting control back to a minimum, with a punchy failure effect of about a second, because fast retries make players tolerate much more difficulty.
takeaways: Quick retries raise tolerance for difficulty and hardship
Interest cools fast between failing and regaining control
Make the failure effect flashy but about one second
Infinite respawns in place make a game feel mindless
Don't respawn players into immediate enemy attacks

principles.principle: Minimize time from failure to regained control
principles.why: Player interest cools quickly between thinking "I blew it" and getting control back; the longer the wait, the more they lose interest, while quick retries raise tolerance for difficulty.
principles.how: Measure death-to-control time, trim the death presentation and load times, and hand control back immediately; if text must remain, let button presses advance it.
principles.anti_pattern: Long death sequences, slow fades and loading screens before a retry.
principles.quote: I'm talking about the time between when the player thinks, "Ugh, I blew it!" and when they actually get control again.

principles.principle: Make losing feel impactful, but keep it to about a second
principles.why: Players should really feel the loss, but dragging out the effect wastes the window when their interest is cooling.
principles.how: Play a flashy, impactful failure effect lasting about one second (depending on genre), then return control as soon as possible.
principles.anti_pattern: Dragging out the failure presentation.
principles.quote: When the player loses, they should really feel it. Make the effect flashy and impactful, but get it over with quickly.

principles.principle: Keep a real cost to failure; avoid mindless in-place respawns
principles.why: Infinite chances to respawn right where you died can make the game feel mindless, so speed must be balanced against penalty.
principles.how: Pick a middle ground on checkpoint distance and penalties that suits your game's intent.
principles.anti_pattern: Unlimited respawns at the exact spot of death.

principles.principle: Don't let enemies hit players the moment they respawn
principles.why: If players keep losing without even touching the controller, they won't want to try anymore.
principles.how: Place respawn points where no enemy can attack the player right away.
principles.anti_pattern: Respawning players into enemy fire.

summary: Start making games with whatever tool you can get, and tinker with simple movement code such as inertia, because that hands-on experimenting is how you learn what shapes game feel.
takeaways: Family BASIC made Sakurai realize he could make games
Only 2 KB of program space; presets saved memory
Experimenting with sprite inertia taught him game feel
Most important: sit down and try making a game

principles.principle: Learn game feel by tweaking movement code like inertia yourself
principles.why: Toying with sprite inertia in Family BASIC let Sakurai see how different changes affect a game's feel, knowledge he drew on for Kirby's Dream Land.
principles.how: Build a tiny controllable-character prototype and vary inertia and acceleration one value at a time, noting how each change feels.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on a convenient high-level movement command when you need responsive control; MOVE was limited to eight directions and lagged on input.
principles.example: Family BASIC's SPRITE command: a controller-driven sprite with a little inertia.

principles.principle: Start by sitting down and making a game with available tools
principles.why: Family BASIC, bought with six months of allowance, is what showed Sakurai he could make games; without it there would be no Kirby or Smash Bros.
principles.how: Pick whatever tool is accessible now and finish something small instead of waiting for better equipment.
principles.anti_pattern: Waiting for ideal hardware or tools before starting.
principles.example: Family BASIC on the Famicom.
principles.quote: But the most important thing to do is to first sit down and try to make a game.

principles.principle: Use built-in assets so scarce resources go to behavior
principles.why: With only 2 KB of program space, coding your own pixel art would use it all up; Family BASIC's character presets made moving characters easy.
principles.how: When memory or time is tight, use presets or placeholder art and spend your budget on movement and logic.
principles.example: Family BASIC presets: Mario, Pauline and Luigi's palette.

summary: Design your map as a real game screen and put navigation information into the main view, so players look at your world instead of staring at the mini-map.
takeaways: Players often watch the mini-map instead of the world
Constantly toggling a full-screen map is frustrating
Mystery Dungeon overlays a translucent map on the screen
Put guidance on the game screen, like Forza's corner cues
Anticipate where players look and what they think

principles.principle: Design maps so players watch the world, not the corner map
principles.why: When the mini-map holds the player's gaze, the huge, beautifully rendered game screen goes to waste; opening and closing a full map over and over is frustrating.
principles.how: Try a translucent full-screen map overlay usable while playing, with one button to switch to map-only view.
principles.anti_pattern: Making players repeatedly open and close a full-screen map.
principles.example: Mystery Dungeon series: translucent map over the whole screen.
principles.quote: It's important to consider where players will look while they're playing your game. And it's even more important to anticipate what they'll be thinking.

principles.principle: Put navigation information directly on the game screen
principles.why: On-screen guidance tells players what they need without a glance at the map, as Forza's visual guidance shows how tight a corner is.
principles.how: Add in-world markers or overlays (e.g., cues for upcoming corner sharpness) for the information players would otherwise read off the map.
principles.example: Forza's visual racing guidance.

principles.principle: Shape terrain to guide players around corners and into areas
principles.why: Positioning and depicting terrain well guides players without relying on the map at all.
principles.how: Lay out landmarks and terrain so they naturally lead players around corners and toward interesting areas; plan how vertical spaces read.
principles.example: Subnautica's map struggles to show vertical 3D space.

summary: Give spectators a reason to back one side, even a tiny wager, because a contest is far more exciting to watch when you care who wins.
takeaways: Watching is exciting when you're invested in a side
Smash spectators wager small points; investment, not payout, matters
Recognizable players strengthen the urge to root
Gambling depictions need per-country adjustments
Choosing among 2-3 draws beats purely random gacha

principles.principle: Let spectators pick a side before the match starts
principles.why: In a contest only one side can win, and having someone to root for makes it far more exciting; Smash's small point wagers work because they create investment, not because of the points.
principles.how: Before a replay or spectated match, ask viewers to predict the winner with a small wager, and show identifying info about the players.
principles.anti_pattern: Spectator modes that give viewers no stake in the outcome.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. online spectator mode with point wagers.
principles.quote: In a contest between two sides where only one can win, you'll find yourself more fired up if you have someone to root for going in.

principles.principle: Offer two or three meaningful choices instead of purely random draws
principles.why: Choosing among a few draws, with a reason the choice carries weight, has more meaningful impact on players than pure randomness.
principles.how: In gacha or random rewards, present 2-3 options and give each a reason that makes picking it matter.
principles.anti_pattern: Purely random draws with no player choice.
principles.example: Free-to-play gacha (his suggested application).

principles.principle: Check every region's gambling rules before shipping wager features
principles.why: Countries regulate depictions of gambling differently, and Smash's spectator mode needed careful, repeated adjustments to comply; it's tougher than you might think.
principles.how: Research regional rules early for any betting-like feature and budget time for several rounds of adjustment.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. spectator mode.

summary: Don't overlook scaling in animation: squash and stretch while keeping the object's volume about the same gives things texture, life and a physical presence.
takeaways: Scaling is underused next to rotation and translation
Squash and stretch gives objects texture and life
Keep mass constant: squash vertically, stretch horizontally
Pure vertical squash made 3D Kirby lose presence

principles.principle: Use squash and stretch to give objects texture and life
principles.why: Rotation and translation are commonplace, but adding scaling makes a bouncing ball feel totally different, almost touchable; it can really punch up animation.
principles.how: Add squash to landings, crouches and bounces, then compare the animation with and without scaling.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating rotation and translation as the whole toolkit.
principles.example: A bouncing-ball GIF shown with and without scaling; Kirby's crouch and landing squash since Game Boy.

principles.principle: Preserve volume: widen whenever you squash
principles.why: Keeping mass roughly constant sells the squash; when 3D Kirby was only squashed vertically he lost physical presence, so Sakurai asked for more volume on the sides.
principles.how: Stretch horizontally when squashing vertically; on 3D models shape a squashed pose (oval-track profile, or a blend shape) instead of just scaling one axis.
principles.anti_pattern: Squashing on one axis only, so the shape loses volume and looks dull.
principles.example: Kirby's 3D model, per a Daily Report image asking for side volume.
principles.quote: A key rule to follow with this technique is to always keep the object's mass roughly the same.

summary: A demo is one of the best ways to get a game noticed, but plan it like a small separate game: strip out spoiler data, maintain and test a second build, and only ship it once it is balanced.
takeaways: Demos draw players when publicity alone isn't enough
A demo can become almost another small game
Remove spoiler data; players will find it
Two builds mean double management, tuning and QA
A half-baked demo invites negative word of mouth

principles.principle: Budget a demo as a separate small game, not a quick slice
principles.why: From the moment you decide on a demo you maintain two versions with separate management, updates, tuning and QA, and anything public needs nearly final-level testing.
principles.how: Schedule the demo as its own deliverable with its own tuning, update and QA passes.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming a demo is just a piece carved off the full game.
principles.quote: If you're not careful, it can be almost like creating another small game.

principles.principle: Strip spoiler data from pre-release demos, then retest thoroughly
principles.why: People can and likely will find spoiler data left in a demo, and removing data greatly increases the chance of something breaking.
principles.how: Keep spoiler content in separable files so it can be removed cleanly, audit the demo build, and run full QA after removal.
principles.anti_pattern: Shipping a demo build with leftover spoiler data.

principles.principle: Only release a demo balanced enough to represent the final game
principles.why: A half-baked demo increases the risk of players writing you off, and negative word of mouth turns away potential players.
principles.how: If the pre-release build isn't balanced, consider a post-launch demo made from the finished game, accepting a smaller splash.
principles.anti_pattern: Rushing out an unbalanced demo on the idea that something is better than nothing.

principles.principle: Work to make your game known; demos are highly effective
principles.why: Most games go unnoticed and publicity alone usually isn't enough; downloadable demos may be more effective than ever.
principles.how: Weigh a demo early in your marketing plan, deciding between pre-launch impact and post-launch ease.
principles.quote: Still, demos can be very effective, and in the end, it's absolutely better to be known than to be unknown.

summary: As a director, post a daily internal report (a screenshot plus 3-5 varied topics, open to comments), because it builds trust, gets read where email doesn't, and keeps the whole team seeing the big picture.
takeaways: Daily report: screenshot on top, then 3-5 topics
Helps an outside director stop being a stranger
Gets read more reliably than team-wide email
Daily screenshot doubles as a whole-team progress report
An opinions board collects suggestions easily

principles.principle: Post a daily internal report with a screenshot and 3-5 topics
principles.why: Team-wide emails often go unread, but a page with something new every day is one people keep up with on their own, making it a more reliable channel.
principles.how: Each workday, post a current screenshot plus news, your work, checklists and issues to fix, with comments enabled; use it for key announcements.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on mass email for important information.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Brawl onward; a Sephiroth reveal via the report crashed the server.
principles.quote: However, the Daily Report offers something new every day— so most people take it upon themselves to keep up with it

principles.principle: Let the team know you personally, especially as an outside director
principles.why: Taking direction from an unknown outsider doesn't feel good; reading his reports meant Sakurai was no longer a total stranger.
principles.how: Mix non-work topics into your reports (games you played, current events, your thoughts) and vary them daily.
principles.example: Sakurai joining existing teams as a freelance director.

principles.principle: Show everyone the whole game's progress every day
principles.why: On big teams each person's work is one small part, and they can lose sight of the bigger picture without seeing what others make.
principles.how: Share a daily screenshot of the current build and invite members to post what they finished that day.
principles.example: Screenshot of the Day, later shared publicly on Twitter.

principles.principle: Give the team an easy channel for suggestions and requests
principles.why: Sakurai set up an "opinions board" when joining teams and found it effective for gathering input.
principles.how: Create a simple board where anyone can submit suggestions and requests at any time.

summary: What we love as children shapes our tastes as adults, so remember your game may be shaping someone's childhood, and that direct control of a bright, flashy screen is what leaves a lasting impression.
takeaways: Dial-controlled Pong-style games left a lasting impression
200 yen meant choosing each 50-yen game carefully
Childhood loves shape our tastes as adults
Smash Ultimate topped a 2019 children's survey

principles.principle: Make the first moments of control direct, bright and flashy
principles.why: Twisting a dial to move objects directly on a bright, flashy screen is what impressed young Sakurai about his first video games.
principles.how: Make sure the player's first input immediately moves something clearly visible on an eye-catching screen.
principles.example: Pong-style potentiometer games.

principles.principle: Remember your game may shape a child's lifelong tastes
principles.why: The things we love as kids, and the joy they bring, strongly shape our adult tastes, and creators may have that effect on today's children.
principles.how: Keep young players in mind as an audience whose experience with your game may stay with them for life.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate as the top game in CoroCoro Comic's 2019 survey.
principles.quote: I'd say that the things we love as kids and the joy those things bring us go on to have a huge impact on our tastes in adulthood.

summary: Build your concept from what the hardware uniquely offers and what the market lacks, then shape every system (opening, enemy size, controls, story delivery) around how and where the game will actually be played.
takeaways: Aimed at hardcore players since casual was already covered
Rail-shooter openings avoid overwhelming beginners
Enemies 4-5x Pit's size for a small screen
Story told during play like a radio program
108 weapons treated like characters, affecting speed too

principles.principle: Aim your concept at the hardware's strengths and the market gap
principles.why: Touch! Generations already covered casual DS players, so Sakurai made a meaty game for hardcore players, and glasses-free 3D made depth central, leading to a TPS reimagined like Smash reimagined fighting games.
principles.how: List what the platform uniquely does and which audiences are already served, then target the gap and rethink the genre's by-the-book conventions.
principles.anti_pattern: Making a genre game that follows by-the-book theory.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising on the 3DS.

principles.principle: Open with a simpler mode before demanding the full control set
principles.why: Starting with the TPS land battles would force beginners to learn dodging, aiming and firing at once; the rail-shooter air battle eases them in with simple shooting and quick scenery changes.
principles.how: Begin levels or the game with a constrained version of the core action, and add free movement and dodging after.
principles.anti_pattern: An opening that requires every control skill at once.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's air battles before land battles.
principles.quote: Starting with the TPS portion would've required the player to immediately learn how to dodge, aim, and fire— which would be a lot for beginners.

principles.principle: Size enemies for the screen the game is played on
principles.why: Focusing on a tiny part of the screen to hit distant targets suits a handheld poorly, so Uprising made enemies many times larger than normal.
principles.how: On small screens, scale enemies well above genre norms (Uprising's standard enemies are four to five times Pit's size).
principles.anti_pattern: Requiring pinpoint aim at tiny distant targets on a portable screen.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising land battles.

principles.principle: Tell the story during gameplay instead of briefings and cutscenes
principles.why: Uprising's story unfolds as you play, like a radio program; because air battles had to match story beats exactly, Sakurai wrote the scenario on the development side.
principles.how: Deliver story as in-play dialogue with an option to turn it off, and write it in-house when beats must sync with fixed-length gameplay and music.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's in-play dialogue.

summary: Make broad input (many games and media, taken in thoughtfully) and steady output (writing and sharing on a schedule) daily habits, because that's how a director keeps their work on par with modern games.
takeaways: Make both input and output daily habits
Play many games, and try to see the endings
Output: Famitsu column, Daily Report, screenshots, YouTube
Reflect on media so it doesn't pass through you

principles.principle: Play many current games and finish them to know the bar
principles.why: Sakurai needs to grasp the scope of modern games so what he delivers can be on par; he calls it a must.
principles.how: Play as many different games as you can rather than one at length, and try to reach each ending.
principles.anti_pattern: Sinking all your play time into a single title.

principles.principle: Make regular output a long-term habit
principles.why: Sakurai pairs input with habitual output (an 18-year-9-month Famitsu column, a daily team report, a daily screenshot, this channel); staying active with both, he says, lets you achieve great things.
principles.how: Commit to a recurring output such as a weekly column or daily team report, and keep it going.
principles.example: Weekly Famitsu column; Daily Report; Screenshot of the Day.
principles.quote: Take a lot in, put a lot out. Stay active with both, and I think you can achieve great things.

principles.principle: Reflect actively on whatever media you consume
principles.why: Watching something can be very impactful if you reflect on its facets while you do; input you don't think about is wasted.
principles.how: Choose the input form that suits you and note what works and why while playing or watching.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting media go in one ear and out the other.
principles.quote: make sure the media you consume doesn't go in one ear and out the other.

summary: When commissioning arrangements, give composers clear gameplay-driven rules, let them pick pieces they connect with, review through a sound director, and never lose the original melody.
takeaways: Pick many more candidate songs than you'll use
Intro for the countdown, big shifts, climax at end
Fit arrangements to 2-2.5 minute timed matches
Route feedback through the sound director
Keep the main melody so humming matches the original

principles.principle: Keep the original main melody intact in every arrangement
principles.why: Players come to hear this one song out of many; arrangements that change the piece totally disappoint, like the Star Wars theme changing with each film.
principles.how: Require that humming the arrangement is like humming the original, and flag mistranscriptions in review.
principles.anti_pattern: Changing a melody because the original feels antiquated.
principles.example: Disappointing game-music arrangement CDs; the Star Wars theme analogy.
principles.quote: Even if the original feels antiquated to you, and even if you have the urge to change it, make sure you maintain the piece's identity.

principles.principle: Brief arrangers with structural rules drawn from gameplay
principles.why: Smash needs competitive tempo and energy, an intro for the "3, 2, 1, GO!" countdown, big shifts for a dynamic game, a climax, and a length fitting two-minute (2.5 in Ultimate) timed matches.
principles.how: Give composers a written brief: tempo, intro or post-countdown start, dynamic shifts, end-climax, loop point and target length matching a typical match.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. arrangement guidelines.

principles.principle: Route music feedback through someone with musical vocabulary
principles.why: Sakurai may know how he wants something but lack the musical language to express it, so passing feedback through the sound director gets the best results.
principles.how: Run several review rounds covering tempo, intonation, transcription accuracy and direction, delivered via your sound director.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's sound director.

principles.principle: Match each piece to a composer's attachment or strengths
principles.why: It's best when composers arrange a piece they have an attachment to; even versatile composers have areas where they excel most.
principles.how: Let composers choose first; when assigning, pick the piece that best suits each composer's strengths.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. arrangement assignments.

summary: If failure sends players back to the start, your game must keep showing them something they want to see next, so plan what stuck players will face on every retry instead of copying hard-game systems and hoping they persist.
takeaways: Start-over mechanics suit indies but need real appeal
Players repeat only if they want to see what's next
Ask what scenery stuck players will see repeatedly
Being able to scrape by yourself proves nothing

principles.principle: Give players something they want to see next before forcing restarts
principles.why: Most players won't enjoy repeating the same content endlessly; they continue out of a desire to see what comes next, so the game must show them something to look forward to.
principles.how: Make upcoming content visible or hinted, and add variety (randomized equipment, items, events) to the repeated parts.
principles.anti_pattern: Mimicking Souls-like or permadeath systems without creating the pull to push on.
principles.example: Dark Souls players push on to reach what's next, partly from trust in FromSoftware.
principles.quote: In other words, the game itself needs to be appealing enough to make players want to push on.

principles.principle: Plan what stuck players will see on repeated attempts
principles.why: If more players than expected hit a wall, they may keep seeing the same things again and again and quit.
principles.how: For each likely failure point, list what players replay on the way back, then shorten it or vary it.
principles.anti_pattern: Low-variety content that players must repeat many times.

principles.principle: Don't judge difficulty by your own ability to scrape by
principles.why: What keeps players going depends on volume, story and how fleshed out the game is, not on other games being hard or on the developer clearing it.
principles.how: Test difficulty with players outside the team and assume more of them will hit walls than you expect.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming players will persist because hard games are popular.
principles.quote: just because other games are hard, or because you can scrape by in the game you created, don't assume players will want to stick with it.

summary: 3D motion sickness comes from on-screen motion that your inner ear doesn't feel, so offer options to tone down camera embellishments like footstep shake and inertial sway, and test with people who actually get sick.
takeaways: Sickness comes from eyes and inner ear disagreeing
Offer a toggle for footstep vertical camera shake
Lock on-screen vehicle frames without inertial movement
Less embellishment means less sickness, but less entertainment
Test with team members prone to motion sickness

principles.principle: Offer toggles for camera shake and other inertial embellishments
principles.why: Sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear doesn't feel; turning off footstep shake can be very effective, but removing presentation for everyone makes the game less entertaining.
principles.how: Add options to disable footstep vertical shake and other inertia-heavy camera effects rather than stripping presentation for everyone.
principles.anti_pattern: Shipping strong camera inertia with no way to turn it off.
principles.example: The common FPS option to toggle vertical shake from footsteps.
principles.quote: Look at your game's presentation, and you'll find there's no harm in including options to counteract motion sickness.

principles.principle: Lock on-screen vehicle frames in place, without inertial movement
principles.why: A vehicle frame that sways adds visual motion with no matching physical motion; fixing it on screen reduces sickness.
principles.how: Offer a mode where cockpit or vehicle frames are simply drawn on screen and don't move.

principles.principle: Test camera comfort with players prone to motion sickness
principles.why: Motion sickness varies greatly between people, so a team where nobody suffers from it will struggle to catch the problem.
principles.how: Recruit testers who get 3D motion sickness and review camera options with them.
principles.anti_pattern: Signing off camera comfort based on a team that never feels sick.

summary: Unify your game's look by starting from a few image boards by your best artist and having everyone, whatever their personal specialty, build to that single visual concept.
takeaways: Artists must match the team's style, whatever their specialty
A few image boards by a top artist set direction
Models and lighting built from boards iron out differences
Denim on Mario's overalls bridges realistic and cartoony

principles.principle: Set the look with a few image boards before production
principles.why: Image boards by an exceptional artist give the team a base for models and lighting, ironing out skill and style differences and pointing everyone the same way.
principles.how: Have your strongest artist paint the world, scenery, characters and items first, and review all assets against those boards.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting each artist work in their own preferred style.
principles.quote: Start with a singular visual concept, then execute on that concept with skilled art. That's the way that countless games come together.

principles.principle: Bridge mixed art styles with shared material detail
principles.why: Smash mixes realistic and cartoony characters; without unifying them it might look like a fight between live action and animation.
principles.how: Add realistic material textures to stylized characters (e.g., denim on cartoony overalls) so they sit beside realistic ones.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving characters from different sources in clashing styles.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: denim texture on Mario's overalls.

principles.principle: Expect every artist to match the set style outside their specialty
principles.why: Team members must produce the same visual style, so specialists sometimes make art outside their strengths; most artists are very good at matching a set style, and competition demands it.
principles.how: Practice working in styles beyond your favorite, and budget for unification, which costs more as visual fidelity rises.

summary: Build hit marks to a checklist (flashiness that matches the impact, visual balance, correct placement, layered elements, not hiding characters, fitting duration, and both bright and dark tones), and use hitstop to animate them in more detail.
takeaways: Hit-mark flashiness should match the hit's impact
Place marks where attack and target hitboxes meet
Layer shockwave, upward spray and material-specific sparks
Include dark tones so marks read on bright backgrounds
Keep animating hit marks during hitstop

principles.principle: Match hit-mark flashiness and duration to the hit's impact
principles.why: Hit marks exist for clear visual feedback and fun, so flashy is generally best, but quick repeated hits need short effects and even long ones should resolve fairly quickly.
principles.how: Tie effect size and lifetime to damage or attack strength; keep multi-hit effects brief and tune style to the title (cartoony vs. realistic).
principles.anti_pattern: Hit marks that cover the characters or clutter the screen.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's range of hit marks.

principles.principle: Include dark tones so hit marks read on any background
principles.why: Purely additive or weak-contrast effects feel lacking, and all-bright effects aren't visible enough on light backgrounds.
principles.how: Pair bright additive layers with a dark element, such as a dark backdrop, and check the mark on light and dark stages.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying only on additive blending.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate hit marks with a dark backdrop.
principles.quote: Exclusively bright effects won't be visible enough on a lighter background, so it's good to include some dark colors as well.

principles.principle: Spawn hit marks at the real hitbox contact point
principles.why: A hit happens where attack and target hitboxes meet; if that isn't checked correctly, the mark appears in a strange spot, especially with large hitboxes.
principles.how: Compute the effect position from the overlapping hitboxes and add layered elements there (shockwave behind, upward spray, sparks for machines).
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: pulled-back camera means large hitboxes.

principles.principle: Keep hit-mark animations running through hitstop
principles.why: Characters freeze during hitstop but effects can keep animating, so that window can carry extra detail.
principles.how: Exclude hit-mark particles from the hitstop freeze and design them to unfold during it.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate; its hitstop direction-input effect shows the adjusted flight path.
principles.quote: In most cases, hit marks can continue their animations even during the hit stop, so you should use that time to pack in even more detailed presentation.

summary: When a project truly needs you, commit fully (clear your other work) and use the time before the team arrives to write the design docs and win over stakeholders, because a series' spirit depends on whoever holds it together.
takeaways: Brawl was announced before development or a director existed
Iwata's fallback: Melee's 26 fighters plus network support
Sakurai cleared other projects to commit fully
Design docs and creator pitches done before October start
Core team from Game Arts, growing past 100 people

principles.principle: Commit fully: clear other work when a project needs all of you
principles.why: Making a Smash Bros. would require all of Sakurai's time, so he turned down his other projects except one already in progress.
principles.how: Before accepting a demanding lead role, decline or finish competing commitments instead of splitting your focus.
principles.anti_pattern: Taking a project that needs everything while juggling other agreements.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl; only Mushiking was kept.
principles.quote: There I was with a task only I could do, and people were looking to me to do it.

principles.principle: Use pre-production to write design docs and win stakeholder buy-in
principles.why: Between E3 and the October start of development, Sakurai wrote the design docs and pitched each character to its original creator, so the team could begin with a plan.
principles.how: In the gap before full staffing, finish your design documents and get approval from rights holders or key stakeholders.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl pre-production.

principles.principle: Build the core team from people who love the game
principles.why: The Game Arts core team had played so much Melee their stick ridges were worn down, and both executives and developers were excited for the project.
principles.how: When recruiting a core team, favor people who know and are enthusiastic about the series or genre.
principles.example: Game Arts staff for Super Smash Bros. Brawl.

summary: If it suits your game's tone, give each menu section its own color and carry it into the submenus, because color and pictures are understood faster than text, but never mix a jumble of colors on one screen.
takeaways: Color-code each menu section and its submenus
Pictures are recognized faster than text, intuitively
Avoid a mishmash of colors on one screen
Heavy color can make a game look aimed at kids
Tone and manner take top priority

principles.principle: Color-code each menu section and carry the color into submenus
principles.why: Pictures and color convey more information than words and are understood through intuition, while text has to be read before it's understood.
principles.how: Assign each top-level menu a color (Smash: red, Spirits: green) and theme all its submenus to match; use large images on panels.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate main menu.
principles.quote: Compared to text, pictures can be recognized much faster, and parsed largely through intuition.

principles.principle: Avoid a mishmash of colors on a single screen
principles.why: Mixing many colors on one screen often results in a mess, depending on design quality and direction.
principles.how: Keep one dominant color theme per screen; large character art can be the exception, since the images become memorable.
principles.anti_pattern: A jumble of competing colors on one screen.
principles.example: Smash for 3DS/Wii U's character-art panels mixed colors but stayed readable.

principles.principle: Let the game's tone decide how much color the UI uses
principles.why: Lots of color can make a game feel aimed at younger audiences; any color choice works if it matches the game's atmosphere.
principles.how: Choose palette saturation to fit your tone and audience before applying color-coding.
principles.anti_pattern: Applying bright color-coding regardless of the game's tone and manner.

summary: Build risk and reward into your systems by tying power to danger (firepower that grows as you close in, rewards placed beside hazards, weapons with real trade-offs), and study why a game is fun instead of copying it.
takeaways: Darius's shot limit rewards fighting up close
Close-range rapid fire kills bosses faster
Gradius puts power-ups beside deadly terrain
Give every weapon clear upsides and downsides
Understand why a game is fun; don't mimic

principles.principle: Make firepower depend on taking positional risks
principles.why: Darius limits how many shots can be on screen, so hanging back uses up your shots while moving close lets you fire far more; staying back against bosses means less reward.
principles.how: Cap on-screen player projectiles so effective fire rate rises as the player approaches enemies, and let aggressive positioning kill bosses faster.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting the player easily wipe every enemy from safety, which has no push and pull.
principles.example: Darius (Genesis version): shot limit, bombs and boss fights.

principles.principle: Give every weapon choice a real upside and downside
principles.why: When each weapon has pros and cons, choosing one broadens the game essence; this kind of trade-off thinking works in any game.
principles.how: Design options with explicit trade-offs (e.g., better upward coverage but only two shots at a time and weaker straight ahead).
principles.example: Gradius: the double cannon vs. the laser.
principles.quote: What downsides will you accept, and what upsides will you gain? I'd say this kind of thinking can be effective in any game.

principles.principle: Place rewards next to hazards
principles.why: In Gradius, touching terrain costs a life, so enemies and power-ups placed beside terrain turn collecting them into a risk worth a reward.
principles.how: Position power-ups and valuable targets near deadly geometry so getting them requires risk.
principles.example: Gradius: power-ups near terrain.

principles.principle: Understand why a game is fun before borrowing from it
principles.why: Mimicking an existing game won't give yours a unique flavor; and pushing game essence too hard can cost flair or make play a chore.
principles.how: When studying a game you admire, write down the risk/reward structure that makes it fun, then design your own around that reason.
principles.anti_pattern: Copying surface features of an existing game.
principles.quote: don't just mimic an existing game. Instead, think about why that game is fun in the first place.
